hero.title: Helping Auckland audiences get closer to TEDx
hero.intro: TEDxAuckland is an independently run TED event. In 2018 I volunteered to redesign its website. I led the design and ended up running the project, with a team of four over about six months.

image.alt: The TEDxAuckland homepage in a browser window, over a dark photo of the event venue

facts.v: Volunteer. Led the design and ran the project

p: The site from the previous year had been built in CloudCannon by a volunteer, and by the time I saw it, it was broken in enough places to be a problem. It loaded.

blocks.text: There was no clear way to buy a ticket, which for an event site is most of the job.

p: The organisation needed three things from the new site:

items: Reflect the energy of the events
Put speakers in front of a diverse local audience

sections.heading: Quick to find a talk, a speaker or a ticket

blocks.title: Scannability over density
p: I broke the content into clear sections with a strong hierarchy: short blocks instead of long paragraphs, clear headings and spacing, and content modules that are reused across pages.

image.alt: Four talk cards from the Talks page, each with a photo, title, speaker name and topic tags
image.prepare: Talks page, the first two rows of talk cards, cropped tight.
image.caption: Every talk card uses the same module: photo, title, speaker and topic tags.

blocks.title: Easier navigation
p: Speakers, the schedule and tickets are easy to find without digging through dense content.
Buy ticket sits at the right of the menu on every page, and a red strip under each page header names the next event, its date and the venue.

image.alt: Top of the TEDxAuckland homepage: menu, Buy ticket link, hero and the red upcoming event strip
image.prepare: Homepage, from the menu down to the red upcoming event strip and the start of the speaker row.
image.caption: The menu, the ticket link and the next event are visible before any scrolling.

blocks.title: A stronger focus on speakers
p: Speakers are one of the main reasons people attend TEDx events. Choosing a speaker opens their bio, links and talk in place, so people can explore the line-up without leaving the page.

image.alt: A speaker selected in the grid, with her bio, links and talk video opened below
image.prepare: People page: the first speaker row with one speaker selected and the panel open below it.
image.caption: Speaker details open inside the grid. Portraits are black and white until one is selected.

blocks.title: More than one way in
p: The homepage supports several entry points. People can browse by speaker, by topic and theme, or by previous talks, so they start from what they care about most instead of following a single path to the ticket.

image.alt: The most popular talks banner and the talk filter, with Popular, Category and Years tabs and hashtag topics
image.prepare: Talks page: the red 'most popular talks' band and the filter below it, with the hashtag topics.
image.caption: Talks can be filtered by popularity, category, year or topic.

p: I kept the palette close to the TED brand: black and charcoal backgrounds, white type, and [[one red for actions and event information]]. Main headings are set in Noe Display Bold and subheadings in Gotham Bold.

p: Ticket purchasing inside the site got complicated quickly. There were four of us, all volunteers, so we did not have the resource to build it properly, and ticketing moved to a third party. {{Name the ticketing provider if you can.}}
The site still carries the rest of the flow:

blocks.text: Only the last step happens somewhere else.

sections.heading: Nobody had said who was doing what

p: I had only worked in agencies, where everyone knows their role and the work moves without anyone having to ask. I turned up expecting that.

The producer was not used to working that way. He was not certain what needed doing, who should do it, or by when, and he assumed I would take care of all of it. So things sat still until I noticed they had.

What fixed it was a meeting where I said out loud what was missing and where we needed to get to. After that we had regular meetings, a timeline and deadlines. The producer took on the sponsors, briefed the copywriter, chased photographers for images and video, and pulled together the speakers and their details. Once people could see the whole project and their part in it, it moved.

blocks.text: The lesson was not about design.

p: On a volunteer team nobody is anyone's boss and every deadline is optional, so [[someone has to say who is doing what, and when]]. That was my job, and it took me too long to work out that it was.
